Dimensionally and morphologically driven effects of nanomaterials on the enhancement of electroanalytical sensing performance: A review
abstract: Electrochemical sensors are widely used in environmental monitoring, clinical diagnostics, and food-safety assessment because they can support rapid analysis, relatively low-cost instrumentation, and sensitive detection when sensing interfaces and recognition strategies are appropriately designed. Bare electrodes, however, may show slow electron-transfer kinetics, limited electroactive area, or insufficient stability. Incorporating nanomaterials can address these constraints by modifying charge transport, active-site accessibility, analyte accumulation, and interfacial chemistry. This review uses dimensionality and morphology as operational descriptors to examine how zero-dimensional (0D), one-dimensional (1D), two-dimensional (2D), and three-dimensional (3D)/hierarchical architectures influence structure-dependent electroanalytical behavior. 0D materials provide discrete catalytic or redox-active sites and, in selected nanoclusters and quantum dots, size-dependent electronic effects. 1D architectures can support directional or percolated charge transport, subject to orientation, connectivity, junction resistance, and electrode adhesion. 2D materials provide accessible interfaces, exposed basal, edge, or defect sites, and tunable surface chemistry, including selected ultrathin nanosheets and nanofilms. 3D/hierarchical architectures regulate analyte-accessible reaction volumes and spatially partition functions: hollow and nanoporous structures organize internal transport, core–shell structures provide radial partitioning, and Janus interfaces provide lateral or anisotropic partitioning. Representative studies are compared using unified analytical and structure-related criteria, while experimentally supported mechanisms are distinguished from plausible structure-based interpretations. The resulting trends are discussed across environmental, food, and biomedical applications without treating dimensionality as a universal performance ranking. Despite substantial advances in nanoscience, challenges remain in colloidal and structural stability, reproducible fabrication, complex-matrix interference, scalability, and device integration. Future progress will require mechanistically supported interface design, greener and more reproducible manufacturing, and experimentally validated artificial intelligence (AI)- or machine learning (ML)-assisted workflows for materials optimization and signal interpretation. Future progress will require mechanistically supported interface design, greener, more reproducible manufacturing, and clearer integration of artificial intelligence/machine learning (AI/ML) approaches, in which transferable materials-design precedents are distinguished from experimentally validated electrochemical sensing and signal-interpretation workflows.

One Health water-based epidemiology: The chemical perspective
abstract: One Health water-based epidemiology (OH-WBE) is a valuable tool for assessing both public and environmental health aligning with the One Health ethos. OH-WBE is proposed as a conceptual extension of wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) as it incorporates all water matrices for the collective assessment of health across humans, animals, and the environment. This review aims to evaluate OH-WBE within this context while providing insight into current challenges and its future. Through an analytical chemistry lens, this work reviews common analytical approaches for completing One Health assessments from selection of sampling sites to sample collection, sample extraction, and instrumental analysis. As both lifestyle and chemical exposure influence community health, biochemical indicators (BCIs) from these categories are discussed focusing on recent applications and novel developments. BCIs indicative of lifestyle include nicotine, caffeine, and food markers, such as artificial sweeteners. Illicit drug consumption, including novel psychoactive substances, pharmaceuticals, and hazardous chemicals are reviewed as BCIs of chemical exposure. While water-based epidemiology has been successfully employed for One Health assessments, there are limitations and considerations which require interdisciplinary collaboration and further research to adequately address. Population normalisation approaches, challenges in selecting appropriate biomarkers and identifying reliable correction factors, and the ethical application of OH-WBE are four themes which are examined. Looking to the future, this work reviews advancements which are needed to enable further adoption of OH-WBE: the discovery and application of endogenous biomarkers; enhanced triangulation of OH-WBE results; embracing of sensing technologies, machine learning, and cloud-based infrastructure to enable real-time data collection and early-warning systems; and the harnessing of high-resolution mass spectrometry for identification and quantification of novel chemicals of concern. Continued collaboration across sectors will make these advancements achievable.

abstract: CRISPR-based biosensors are emerging as powerful tools in precision medicine, enabling rapid and highly specific molecular detection for personalized interventions. Their performance depends on interconnected components. Guide RNA (gRNA) design and optimization improve on-target activity and reduce off-target effects, while Cas protein engineering and structure prediction reveal functional determinants for programmable modification. Meanwhile, biosensor design and signal readout strategies enable portable, quantitative, and multiplexed detection. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have created new opportunities to optimize these components. AI bridges molecular design and analytical performance, enhancing sensitivity, specificity, quantitative readout, and automation in CRISPR-based biosensing. This paper provides a systematic review and comparative analysis of recent progress in AI-enabled gRNA design and optimization, Cas protein engineering and structure prediction, and biosensor readout and automation for CRISPR-based biosensing. It further discusses the opportunities and challenges associated with integrating these advances into multifunctional, standardized platforms for point-of-care testing and clinical translation.

From affinity to kinetics: SPR as the analytical backbone of AI-driven drug discovery
abstract: AI-driven drug discovery can now propose candidates faster than experimental triage can validate. However, many models still rely on static affinity or potency endpoints such as K D , IC 50 , or pEC50. This reliance creates a kinetic blind spot, as pharmacological durability often depends on dissociation kinetics and residence time. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) can transform computational binding hypotheses into reusable, time-resolved learning signals. Here, we define the affinity-to-kinetics gap, link residence time to functional persistence, and analyze two AI-enabled workflows. In PRMT5 library compression, screening reduced 460,000 compounds to a single confirmed SPR binder (K D = 21.5 μM); in TNIK generative design, INS018_055 showed potent SPR affinity (K D = 4.32 nM). Across these cases, SPR functions as a quality-control filter and experimental binding validator rather than a terminal confirmation assay. We identify five requirements for AI-ready SPR data: raw sensorgram retention, consistent fitting, explicit QC labels, experimental provenance, and reusable data schemas. Treating sensorgrams, fit diagnostics, and QC labels as data infrastructure facilitates AI–SPR co-learning, providing a practical route to kinetic-aware, auditable, and reusable decision systems.

abstract: In recent years, micro- and nanoparticles have gained interest due to their applicability to diverse biomedical fields, especially drug delivery. Typical batch methods, including solvent evaporation or homogenization, achieve high production volumes but are often characterized by low reproducibility and high polydispersity. For this reason, microfluidics has recently emerged as a promising method for producing monodisperse, finely controlled, and highly tunable carriers. Depending on the material and device geometry, a wide range of particles can be obtained, spanning from the microscale to the nanoscale and from metallic to biomimetic systems. Microfluidics can reduce waste and costs because of the limited volumes employed, while enhancing throughput through parallelization. This review provides an overview of microfluidic technologies for particle production, ranging from the underlying physical principles, including dimensionless numbers, to market applications. Particular attention is devoted to the latest device geometries and materials, as well as to the implementation of artificial intelligence and emerging autonomous formulation strategies for reducing industrial costs and development times. The strengths, limitations, and potential improvements associated with each geometry and material are critically evaluated and compared to provide a comprehensive understanding of microfluidics for drug-delivery applications. Although substantial progress is still required for microfluidics to become a leading technology for industrial particle production, owing to limitations such as device clogging, chip-material compatibility, and the cost and standardization hurdles of large-scale GMP manufacturing, an increasing number of FDA-approved drug carriers may be produced through this innovative approach in the coming years.

abstract: The future of Point-of-Care Platforms depends upon advancing on-site decision-making capabilities by integrating sensing, signal processing, and interpretation within the same physical architecture rather than treating them as separate stages. Emerging paradigms, such as In-sensor computing and In-memory sensing/computing, can enable such systems by performing bio-signal acquisition and interpretation within the same hardware platform, significantly reducing latency and power consumption while eliminating dependence on external processors and cloud connectivity, making diagnostics more compact and suitable for field deployment. The progress in microfluidics and CRISPR-based molecular detection has already brought the analytical performance up to laboratory standards, offering programmable specificity and sensitivity in the attomolar range. Modern electronic solutions have further enabled continuous and quantitative monitoring at ultra-low power. This review presents modern POCT as a system-level fusion of microfluidic control, biochemical recognition and electronic sensing supported by In-memory intelligence that facilitate reliable and faster clinical decisions ensuring timely therapeutic interventions.

title: Recent advances in the determination of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs in soils: implications to the European Soil Monitoring Law
abstract: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are increasingly detected in soils as a result of wastewater irrigation, sewage sludge application, manure amendment, and diffuse anthropogenic inputs. Despite growing concerns over their persistence, mobility, toxicity, and role in antimicrobial resistance, systematic soil monitoring of NSAIDs remains limited. This review synthesizes recent advances in analytical methodologies for NSAID determination in soils, evaluates quality control performance, and integrates current knowledge on toxicity and soil property interactions within the regulatory context of the EU Soil Monitoring Law. Ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE) and solid-phase extraction (SPE) remain the most widely applied sample preparation techniques, while QuEChERS, pressurized liquid extraction (PLE), and microwave-assisted extraction (MAE) represent increasingly adopted greener alternatives. Liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) dominates targeted analysis, whereas high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS) has advanced non-target screening by enabling the identification of transformation products and complex contaminant mixtures, particularly in amended soils. Detection limits frequently reach low ng/g levels, although matrix effects and method harmonization remain complex challenges. This review also examines ecotoxicological evidence, highlighting impacts on soil microbial communities, enzymatic activity, nutrient cycling, plants and soil fauna. Moreover, it underscores the critical role of soil properties, including pH, texture, mineralogy, organic matter, moisture, temperature, and biodiversity, in controlling NSAIDs sorption, mobility, transformation, and bioavailability. By bridging analytical chemistry and soil science, this work provides a holistic framework to support policymakers and researchers in implementing effective soil monitoring and risk assessment strategies aligned with the EU objective of achieving healthy soils by 2050.

‘Smart’ or ‘intelligent’ household products as low-cost diagnostic tools in global health
abstract: : Smart or intelligent household products represent everyday items that have been transformed into low-cost health monitoring tools. As easy-to-operate and cheap products, they epitomize the cutting-edge point-of-care diagnostics tools, which are no longer confined by the boundaries of the mundane, centralized-laboratory-based diagnostics. This study aims to glean the common household products, ranging from cotton to bandages that have been transformed into point-of-care diagnostic tools. Attempting to review these diagnostic tools also reveals the challenges that thwart their real-world applications in point-of-care diagnostics, which are also the central theme of the study. The challenges of the clinical samples to the sustainability issues associated with the traditional diagnostic tools appear to be the prominent bottlenecks that cripples their point-of-care diagnostic applications. We also provide strategies to mitigate these issues by focusing on the sample pre-treatment aspect, regulatory process to improving user experience. We emphasize artificial intelligence as the primary drive in accelerating the transition of the smart or intelligent household products from bench to at-home customer use.

Recent advances and future perspectives of fluorescent probes for serine hydrolases
abstract: Serine hydrolases (SHs) are a family of enzymes characterized by a catalytic triad consisting of serine, histidine, and aspartate. Alterations in their in vivo activity are closely linked to the development and progression of various diseases, including metabolic disorders, neurological diseases, inflammatory and immune-related conditions, and cancer. Therefore, the development of novel bioanalytical methods capable of monitoring dynamic changes in SH activity within living systems is of significant importance for both disease diagnosis and therapeutic evaluation. In recent years, responsive probes for fluorescence analysis of SHs have advanced rapidly; however, a comprehensive and systematic review summarizing these probes is still lacking. This article overviews recent research advances in the development of fluorescent probes for SHs detection, focusing on key SH subfamilies, including serine esterases (e.g., acetylcholinesterase, butyrylcholinesterase, carboxylesterases, and lipases), serine proteases (e.g., chymotrypsin, neutrophil elastase, and trypsin), and serine carboxypeptidases. It discusses the chemical structures and the response mechanisms of the probes, as well as their emerging biomedical applications. This review also highlights several current challenges in the development of fluorescent probes for SHs and discusses future research directions, with the aim of elucidating the pathophysiological significance of SHs and promoting their broader applications in biomedical diagnostics and translational research.

Microneedle-based electrochemical sensors for in planta chemical sensing: From analytical principles to field deployment
abstract: ABSTRACT By 2050, the global population is projected to approach 10 billion, requiring substantial increases in crop productivity under growing land, water, and climate constraints. In this context, plant wearables have emerged as powerful AgriTech tools, highlighted by the inclusion of wearable plant sensors in the World Economic Forum’s Top 10 Emerging Technologies report of 2023 and autonomous biochemical sensing in 2025. Among these technologies, microneedle (MN) electrochemical sensors provide minimally invasive access to plant biofluids and are rapidly becoming a promising platform for real-time chemical monitoring in living plants. In this review, we examine the key design requirements, analytical challenges, and applications of MN-based in-planta sensors for monitoring nutrients, agrochemicals, phytohormones, growth precursors, and stress biomarkers. We first discuss the plant–MN interface, relating plant organs, biofluid composition, and tissue mechanics to MN design considerations. We then describe the principal MN architectures and electroanalytical techniques used to develop sensing platforms. Representative case studies illustrate how MN sensors can resolve the spatial and temporal dynamics of target analytes directly in plants, with emphasis on analytical performance under realistic or in vivo conditions. We further assess the main challenges limiting the translation of MN sensors from laboratory prototypes to autonomous systems suitable for field deployment. Finally, we outline opportunities arising from advances in flexible electronics, wireless communication, Internet-of-Things infrastructures, and artificial-intelligence-driven data analysis. Overall, this review provides an analytical framework for microneedle-based plant (bio)sensing and highlights their potential role in next-generation smart agriculture. We analyzed a collection of over 150 references (2016-2026) identified by database searches, pertinent keywords, and recognized contributions in this field.

title: Engineering MXene-polymer interfaces for high-performance analytical sensing and biosensing
abstract: MXenes represent a distinct category of two-dimensional transition metal carbides, nitrides, and carbonitrides with high electrical conductivity, large surface area, and tunable surface chemistry. This makes them promising candidates for a wide range of applications, including catalysis, environmental remediation, energy storage, and biomedicine. However, their practical use is limited by rapid oxidation, nanosheet restacking, and reduced long-term stability, especially in aqueous and biological environments. Integrating MXenes with polymers is an effective strategy for overcoming these limitations. Polymers improve MXene stability, prevent aggregation, and provide functional groups for bioreceptor immobilization, while the MXene promotes efficient charge transfer, significantly improving the electrochemical performance of the sensor interface. This review discusses recent progress in the design and engineering of MXene–polymer interfaces for high-performance analytical sensors and biosensors. Special attention is given to synthesis methods, interfacial interactions, polymer-assisted stabilization, bioreceptor immobilization, and their influence on sensing performance. Current challenges, including reproducibility, stability, real-sample analysis, and practical application, are also highlighted. Finally, we discuss future directions toward multimodal and in vivo-compatible biosensors, positioning MXene-polymer interfaces as a central platform for advancing analytical chemistry.

title: Advances in COFs- and MOFs-engineered separation methods for pharmaceutical and chiral analysis
Design of Experiments (DoE) in sample preparation techniques for analytical chemistry – Current trends and perspectives
abstract: The application of Design of Experiments (DoE) has become an indispensable tool in Analytical Chemistry, particularly for the sample preparation techniques. These techniques involve critical steps aimed at the extraction, purification, concentration, or isolation of target analytes before instrumental analysis. Owing to the many variables that can influence their performance, traditional trial-and-error approaches often prove inefficient, making DoE an essential strategy for developing more robust, reliable, and sustainable analytical methods. This review provides a comprehensive overview of DoE applications in sample preparation techniques reported over the last five years. First, the fundamental principles of experimental design are discussed, including statistical concepts, terminology, major experimental designs, and strategies for model construction, evaluation, validation, and optimization. Subsequently, recent applications involving solid-phase extraction (SPE)- and liquid-liquid extraction (LLE)-based techniques are critically examined, highlighting current trends, advantages, limitations, and recurring shortcomings observed in the literature, particularly those related to statistical validation and multiresponse optimization. In addition to the critical assessment of the reviewed studies, a bibliometric analysis is presented to identify emerging trends, research gaps, and opportunities for future investigations. Advanced and still underexplored experimental approaches for sample preparation are also discussed, including categorical screening designs, mixture designs, combined experimental designs, Definitive Screening Designs (DSDs), and computational tools that can improve the accessibility of these methodologies. Overall, this review provides a critical and up-to-date perspective on the state of the art, highlighting current challenges, opportunities, and future directions for the application of DoE in the development of more efficient sample preparation techniques.

Bringing cationic and zwitterionic PFAS into focus: Chemical diversity, environmental occurrence and current analysis methods
abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are contaminants whose vast chemical diversity poses substantial challenges to environmental monitoring. Among them, cationic and zwitterionic PFAS have largely remained under the radar, with limited information available on their environmental fate and effects. One of the primary challenges in analyzing these precursors is the limited availability of native reference standards and surrogate internal standards, precluding accurate quantification. Some methods originally developed for anionic PFAS underperformed at extracting cationic and zwitterionic PFAS, and these precursors can also transform during sample processing, further confounding the analysis. This paper provides a critical overview of the chemical diversity, origins, environmental occurrence, and analytical methods for cationic and zwitterionic PFAS. The individual steps of the analytical process, including sample collection and pre-treatment strategies, extraction techniques, chromatographic separation, and mass spectrometry detection, are reviewed, with particular attention to method limitations and pitfalls. We also summarize the analytical figures of merit attained in the literature, including limits of detection, extraction efficiency, and matrix effects. This review should be useful to end-users wishing to expand existing PFAS workflows to cationic and zwitterionic compounds.

title: Optical detection of microplastics using organic dyes
abstract: The rapid increase in global plastic production has led to widespread environmental accumulation and the formation of microplastics (MPs), raising concerns regarding their distribution, sources, and ecological impact. Understanding the environmental fate and potential risks associated with MPs requires analytical methods capable of reliably detecting and characterizing these particles across complex environmental matrices. For this, optical techniques are indispensable tools for MP analysis due to their accessibility, relative simplicity, and ability to provide visual information on particle size, morphology, and colour. This review critically examines currently used optical methods for MP detection, with a particular emphasis on fluorescence-based techniques in which organic dyes are used to stain or label MPs. We survey major classes of fluorescent probes used for MP detection, including the widely used Nile Red (NR) dye, other hydrophobic fluorophores, emerging dye systems, and dye-functionalized materials which are designed to improve staining procedure, selectivity, and performance. A focus is also placed on staining methodology, probe-MP interactions, and key performance parameters reported. By critically evaluating existing methodologies, identifying procedural differences across studies, and highlighting key performance parameters, this review aims to clarify the current state of dye-based optical MP detection and outline future directions for the development of novel optical approaches capable of supporting environmental monitoring and MP research.

Mass spectrometry-based salivary lipidomics as a potential approach in glycemic dysregulation research and monitoring: a perspective review
abstract: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) and prediabetes (preT2D) represent major global health challenges and are closely associated with dyslipidemia and metabolic dysfunction. While blood-based lipidomics has provided valuable insights into pathogenic mechanisms and patient stratification, saliva is emerging as a promising alternative biofluid for non-invasive biomarker discovery. This critical perspective review explores the potential of mass spectrometry (MS)-based lipidomic approaches, which offer high molecular specificity, structural resolution, and sensitivity, for investigating and monitoring glycemic dysregulation through salivary lipid profiling. We first summarize evidence on blood lipidomic signatures associated with T2D and preT2D and then discuss the methodological advantages and analytical challenges of salivomics. Furthermore, we examine emerging MS-based comparative studies that demonstrate partial concordance between salivary and circulating lipid profiles, supporting both the technical feasibility and the translational potential of salivary lipidomics, provided that the specific pre-analytical and analytical challenges of salivary lipid analysis are systematically controlled through dedicated workflow optimization. Despite this encouraging framework, a significant knowledge gap remains, as MS-based salivary lipidomics has not yet been systematically applied to dysglycemic populations. Future research should prioritize: i) large-scale, multicenter, clinically well-characterized cohorts; ii) rigorous pre-analytical and analytical standardization; iii) comprehensive cross-biofluid comparisons. Finally, we discuss the prospective integration of validated salivary lipid biomarkers into lab-on-chip platforms for decentralized, cost-effective, and near-real-time diabetes monitoring, although substantial technological and translational challenges remain.

Analytical platforms for breast cancer liquid biopsy: from biomarker detection to molecular stratification and monitoring
abstract: Breast cancer (BC) remains the most frequently diagnosed malignancy among women worldwide, while limitations of imaging-based screening, particularly in dense breast tissue and early-lesions, continue to challenge timely diagnosis. Liquid biopsy offers a complementary, minimally invasive approach for accessing circulating tumor-derived analytes and supporting early detection, molecular classification, and longitudinal monitoring. This review provides a critical overview of innovative analytical methods used for BC biomarker detection in liquid biopsy, situating them alongside established diagnostic assays. Established tissue- and serum-based biomarkers, including hormone receptors, HER2, Ki-67, and CA15-3, are discussed together with emerging analytes such as circulating tumor DNA, circulating tumor cells, microRNAs, extracellular vesicles, and multimodal signatures. Particular attention is given to how BC molecular heterogeneity, biomarker abundance and stability, sample matrix, and pre-analytical processing influence biomarker selection and analytical performance. Established methods, including immunohistochemistry and immunoassays, are benchmarked against digital PCR, next-generation sequencing, mass spectrometry, CRISPR-Cas diagnostics, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy, microfluidics, and electrochemical biosensors. These platforms are compared with emphasis on clinically relevant detection limits, dynamic range, matrix tolerance, throughput, reproducibility, and translational maturity rather than instrumental sensitivity alone. The electrochemical literature on lipocalin-2 is used as a focused case study to compare recognition elements, electrode materials, signal-amplification strategies, and matrix validation across platforms targeting the same biomarker. The review concludes that further progress in BC liquid biopsy will depend less on incremental reductions in detection limits and more on harmonized pre-analytical workflows, standardized reference materials, robust multiplexed strategies, and prospective validation against clinically relevant diagnostic and therapeutic decisions.

title: Corrigendum to “Chromatographic strategies for cannabinoid isolation: Advances, challenges, and analytical perspectives” [Trac. Trends Anal. Chem. 204 (2026) 119091]
Electroantennography: Less common detection method in gas chromatography
abstract: Gas chromatography coupled to electroantennographic detection provides a biologically selective readout that localizes ecologically and behaviorally relevant volatiles in complex mixtures. Despite decades of use, gas chromatography–electroantennographic detection remains underrepresented in analytical applications. It is often implemented as a craft method, with limited consensus on experimental design, validation, and reporting for inter-laboratory comparability. This review clarifies what is the electroantennographic signal and integrates instrumental and methodological choices that influence performance. These choices include effluent splitting and conditioning via flow, temperature, and humidity, antenna preparation and lifetime, electrode and amplifier configuration, noise and drift control, and synchronization with parallel chemical detectors. Platforms coupled to mass spectrometric detection and/or flame ionization detection, approaches for response normalization and objective event calling, and workflows linking bioactive peak detection to structural assignment and quantitative relevance are presented. Practical reporting and quality-control elements, opportunities for shared response libraries and ring trials, and emerging directions including automation, miniaturized interfaces, and biohybrid sensing are proposed.

Beyond single-mode detection: Advances in plasmonic dual-mode SERS-based optical sensing platforms for biomedical diagnostics
abstract: The development of reliable, highly sensitive analytical tools is essential for accurately detecting disease-related biomarkers and improving clinical decision-making. Dual-mode optical sensors that integrate two optical transduction mechanisms into a single platform are a major focus in nanobiotechnology. They serve as reliable tools in biomedicine for rapid, efficient diagnosis and monitoring and are compatible with point-of-care (POC) applications. Compared with single-mode detection approaches, dual-mode sensing assays reduce analytical uncertainty, expand the linear detection range, improve accuracy, and increase operational flexibility. Among the various combinations, surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) coupled with optical techniques such as colorimetry, fluorescence, electrochemiluminescence, or surface plasmon resonance stands out for its ultrasensitivity and compatibility with POC diagnostics and real-time monitoring. Noble-metal nanoparticles, also called plasmonic nanoparticles (PNPs), are attractive options for such applications because they can serve as sensitive SERS platforms while simultaneously modulating a complementary optical signal. This review summarizes recent progress in the development of plasmon-assisted dual-mode SERS-based biosensing platforms for biomedical diagnosis. Particular emphasis is placed on systems that integrate SERS with colorimetric, fluorescence, electrochemiluminescence, and surface plasmon resonance detection methods. The role of PNPs in enhancing signal transduction and enabling complementary detection mechanisms is discussed, along with strategies to improve the analytical performance of the designed assays. Furthermore, the applicability of these platforms for detecting a wide range of biological targets, from clinically relevant protein biomarkers and nucleic acids to metabolites and pathogens, is highlighted.

Analytical and functional characterization of next-generation therapeutics: ADCs, CAR-T cells, rAAVs, mRNA and VLPs
abstract: Emergence of novel therapeutic modalities such as mRNA therapeutics, virus like particles (VLPs), adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors, chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cells, and antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) presents unique challenges for biomanufacturers who thus far have been primarily familiar with peptides, recombinant proteins, and lately monoclonal antibodies. Conventional analytical and functional characterization platforms need significant adaptation to effectively handle the complexity that these new modalities introduce. This review offers a comprehensive overview of current and emerging analytical technologies used to characterize these next-generation therapeutics. The critical quality attributes (CQAs) for each class of products, as well as the analytical and functional methodologies used for characterizing these entities, have been critically discussed. The article focuses primarily on advancements achieved over the last 5 years (2020-2025).
